Title: Check the whole room, not the confident few
Summary: Hands-up questioning usually hears from the same few confident learners. A whole-room response lets every learner show what they know, including those least likely to volunteer.
WhyItWorks: Rosenshine found the most effective teachers ask a large number of questions and check the responses of all learners. Wiliam (2011) adds that when only volunteers answer, the learners who most need help are the ones you hear from least.
Frameworks: Rosenshine 3 and 6; Digital Skills Framework: communicate and collaborate
WatchOutFor:
Asking the question, then taking the first hand that goes up.
Cutting thinking time short. Count to five in your head before "boards up".
PracticeScenario: You ask "What does PPE stand for?" and five hands go up from the same corner of the room. What will you do differently next time?
PracticeAnswer: Switch to a whole-room response. Use mini whiteboards or Plickers, give a fixed thinking time, then everyone shows at once. Afterwards, check in quietly with the learners who got it wrong.
Keywords: answer class confident hands questioning questions quiet up whole

Title: Start every lesson with a daily review
Summary: Open the lesson with five quick questions that reach back to last lesson, last week and last month.
WhyItWorks: Rosenshine's first principle is to begin each lesson with a short review of previous learning. Retrieval practice research (Roediger and Karpicke, 2006) shows that recalling something strengthens memory more than re-reading it.
WatchOutFor:
Letting learners look things up. Retrieval means remembering, not finding.
Questions that everyone gets right every time. They are too easy to strengthen memory.
PracticeScenario: Your group scores well on last lesson's questions but poorly on last month's. What does this tell you, and what will you change?
PracticeAnswer: Earlier learning is fading. Keep spacing questions back to it in each daily review, and briefly revisit the weakest topic before building on it.
Keywords: forget memory recall remember retrieval review revision

Title: Model it step by step, out loud
Summary: Break a task into small steps and model each one, saying your thinking as you go.
WhyItWorks: Rosenshine found effective teachers present new material in small steps and provide models. Cognitive load theory (Sweller, 1988) explains why: working memory can only hold a few new things at once.
VideoTitle: Rosenshine Masterclass II: Sequencing concepts and modelling
WatchOutFor:
Modelling too many steps in one go. Stop and check after each one.
Saying "this" and "here". Anyone who cannot see where you point loses the model.
PracticeScenario: You demonstrate a full wiring task in one go. Learners then make lots of different mistakes. What went wrong, and what will you change?
PracticeAnswer: Too many steps at once overloaded working memory. Model in short chunks, think aloud at each decision, and check understanding before the next step.
Keywords: confused demonstrate explain explanation lost model new steps

Title: Build it properly: headings first, then the Accessibility Checker
Summary: Use real heading styles, then run the Accessibility Checker before you share anything.
WhyItWorks: Screen readers, Immersive Reader and the Navigation Pane all use headings to show the shape of a document (WCAG 2.2, 1.3.1 Info and Relationships). The Accessibility Checker is the first of the Super Six because every other tool relies on a document being built properly.
Frameworks: WCAG 2.2 AA; Super Six: Accessibility Checker
VideoChannel: Digital Accessibility and Inclusion Day, 23 October 2026
WatchOutFor:
Making text bigger and bold instead of using a heading style.
Treating an empty checker list as proof the file is fully accessible.
PracticeScenario: A learner using a screen reader says your 20-page workbook "is one long block". What is the likely cause, and how do you fix it?
PracticeAnswer: The headings are formatted text, not heading styles. Apply Heading 1, 2 and 3, check them in the Navigation Pane, then run the Accessibility Checker.
Keywords: accessibility accessible alt documents headings powerpoint reader screen slides text wcag word

Title: Fix PowerPoint reading order
Summary: A screen reader reads slide items in the order they were added, not the order you see. Put them in the right order.
WhyItWorks: WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.3.2 (Meaningful Sequence) requires content to be read in an order that keeps its meaning. A slide can look perfect and still be badly built.
VideoChannel: Digital Accessibility and Inclusion Day, 23 October 2026
WatchOutFor:
Adding the title last. It will be read last.
Forgetting that the Selection Pane runs in the opposite direction to the Reading Order pane.
PracticeScenario: A slide is read out as "Bring your PPE" before its title. Why, and how do you fix it?
PracticeAnswer: That box was added before the title. Open the Reading Order pane and drag the title to the top of the list.
Keywords: accessibility accessible alt documents headings powerpoint reader screen slides text wcag word

Title: Write alt text that teaches
Summary: If a picture carries information, describe what it tells the learner. If it does not, mark it decorative.
WhyItWorks: WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.1.1 (Non-text Content) requires a text alternative for any image that carries meaning. Without it, a screen reader says nothing, or reads out a file name.
VideoChannel: Digital Accessibility and Inclusion Day, 23 October 2026
WatchOutFor:
Alt text that describes the picture but not the point, such as "photo of a workshop".
Accepting automatic alt text without reading it.
PracticeScenario: A slide showing a correctly footed ladder has the alt text "photo of a workshop". Rewrite it.
PracticeAnswer: For example: "Ladder at an angle of 1 in 4, footed by a second person holding both stiles." It names the safety point the slide is teaching.
Keywords: accessibility accessible alt documents headings powerpoint reader screen slides text wcag word

Title: Share resources learners can find, but cannot change
Summary: Keep slides read-only in Class Materials, name them the same way every time, and get learners to them in three clicks or fewer.
WhyItWorks: Every extra click is a barrier, especially on a phone. A consistent structure lowers the load of finding things, so attention goes on learning. Read-only files protect the master copy everyone relies on.
Frameworks: Digital Skills Framework: file and permission management
WatchOutFor:
Uploading slides to the general Files area, where learners can edit them.
A different folder structure on every course you teach.
PracticeScenario: A learner deleted your slides from the channel's files by mistake. How do you stop it happening again?
PracticeAnswer: Keep your slides in the Class Materials folder, which is read-only for learners, and keep your master copies there.
Keywords: clicks delete edit files find organise share teams

Title: Hinge questions that change what happens next
Summary: One diagnostic question at the turning point of a lesson. Each wrong answer points to a specific misconception, and tells you what to do.
WhyItWorks: Rosenshine's sixth principle is to check for understanding before moving on. Wiliam (2011) describes hinge questions: every learner answers in about a minute, and each wrong option reveals a known misconception, so the teacher can respond within the lesson.
WatchOutFor:
Wrong options nobody would choose. They tell you nothing.
Asking the hinge question, then moving on regardless of the answers.
PracticeScenario: In a hinge question, 40 per cent of the group choose the option that confuses mass and weight. What happens next?
PracticeAnswer: Re-teach that distinction briefly to that group while the rest start an application task. Then check again with a similar question.
Keywords: answer class confident hands questioning questions quiet up whole

Title: From worked example to independent work
Summary: Move learners from a full worked example, through partly completed ones, to independent practice.
WhyItWorks: Worked examples reduce the load on working memory for novices (Sweller and Cooper, 1985). As expertise grows, the same support gets in the way (Kalyuga et al., 2003), so it should fade. Rosenshine calls this guiding practice and providing scaffolds for difficult tasks.
VideoTitle: Rosenshine Masterclass V: Stages of practice
WatchOutFor:
Jumping from the worked example straight to independent work.
Keeping full support for learners who no longer need it.
PracticeScenario: Half the group copy the worked example word for word but cannot do the independent task. What should you change?
PracticeAnswer: Add a partly completed stage between the two, fade one step at a time, and ask learners to explain each step in their own words.
Keywords: autonomy confused demonstrate explain explanation flipped independence independent lost model new scaffold self steps

Title: Recorded recaps learners can return to
Summary: Record your modelling as you teach, so learners have a captioned recap they can rewatch at their own pace.
WhyItWorks: Rosenshine's tenth principle is weekly and monthly review. A recording gives every learner a second route back to the explanation, which UDL calls multiple means of representation. It also supports absent learners without you repeating the lesson.
VideoTitle: Rosenshine Masterclass IV: Daily, weekly and monthly review
WatchOutFor:
Long recordings. Short clips of one model each are far more useful.
Uncorrected automatic captions on technical vocabulary.
PracticeScenario: A learner missed your demonstration last week. How do they catch up without you repeating it?
PracticeAnswer: They watch the captioned recording in the channel, then complete the linked recap quiz. You check the result and follow up if needed.
Keywords: captions dictation dyslexia eal esol forget hearing immersive memory reader reading recall remember retrieval review revision writing

Title: Make Immersive Reader normal for every learner
Summary: Show every learner how to open Immersive Reader and change how text looks and sounds, so nobody has to ask.
WhyItWorks: Immersive Reader is the second of the Super Six expectations. It helps anyone on any day: a learner with dyslexia or visual stress, a learner working in a second language, or someone tired or reading on a phone. Taught to the whole group, nobody needs a diagnosis to use it (UDL).
VideoChannel: Digital Accessibility and Inclusion Day, 23 October 2026
WatchOutFor:
Showing it once at induction and never again.
Offering it only to learners with a support plan.
PracticeScenario: A learner with dyslexia avoids reading tasks, and won't use support "in front of everyone". What helps?
PracticeAnswer: Make it normal for the whole group. Show everyone, use it yourself on screen, and mention it on every reading task, so using it is ordinary.
Keywords: captions dictation dyslexia eal esol hearing immersive reader reading writing

Title: Teach dictation as a normal way to write
Summary: Show every learner how to speak their work instead of typing it, long before any exam.
WhyItWorks: Many people can say far more than they can type. Dictation helps learners with dyslexia or motor difficulties, fluent speakers who write slowly, and anyone with an injured hand. If a learner may use technology in exams, it needs to be their normal way of working first.
VideoChannel: Digital Accessibility and Inclusion Day, 23 October 2026
WatchOutFor:
Introducing dictation for the first time shortly before an exam.
Offering it only to learners with an access arrangement.
PracticeScenario: A learner may be allowed to use speech-to-text in their exam, but has never used dictation. What is the problem, and what do you do?
PracticeAnswer: It has to be their normal way of working first. Start teaching dictation now, use it in real tasks, and talk to the exams team.
Keywords: captions dictation dyslexia eal esol hearing immersive reader reading writing

Title: Captions on, every time
Summary: Turn on live captions when you present, and caption every video you share.
WhyItWorks: Captions are essential for learners who are deaf or hard of hearing (WCAG 2.2, 1.2.2 Captions). They help everyone in a noisy workshop, learners working in a second language, and anyone meeting technical words for the first time.
Frameworks: Super Six: Live Captions; WCAG 2.2 AA
VideoChannel: Digital Accessibility and Inclusion Day, 23 October 2026
WatchOutFor:
Sharing a video with uncorrected automatic captions.
Turning captions off because "nobody needs them".
PracticeScenario: You show a safety video in a noisy workshop and half the group miss the key instruction. What should you do next time?
PracticeAnswer: Use a captioned video and turn captions on before you play it. Check the captions are accurate, and give the key instruction in writing too.
Keywords: captions dictation dyslexia eal esol hearing immersive reader reading writing

Title: Reduce overload: contrast, colour and one idea at a time
Summary: Design slides and handouts that leave room for thinking: strong contrast, no meaning by colour alone, and one idea at a time.
WhyItWorks: Working memory is limited (Sweller, 1988). Mayer (2009) shows people learn better when extra material is removed, key points are signalled, and slides are not read word for word. WCAG 2.2 sets a minimum contrast of 4.5 to 1 for normal text and 3 to 1 for large text.
VideoChannel: Digital Accessibility and Inclusion Day, 23 October 2026
WatchOutFor:
Red and green for right and wrong, with no words.
Full paragraphs on a slide that you also read aloud.
PracticeScenario: Your slide marks correct answers in green and wrong answers in red. Who does this fail, and how do you fix it?
PracticeAnswer: It fails colour-blind learners, screen reader users and anyone using a black and white printout. Add a word or symbol, such as "Correct" and "Incorrect", alongside the colour.
Keywords: accessibility accessible alt confused demonstrate documents explain explanation headings lost model new powerpoint reader screen slides steps text wcag word

Title: Offer more than one way in, and more than one way to show learning
Summary: Give learners choice in how they take in learning and how they show it, while the goal stays the same.
WhyItWorks: Universal Design for Learning (CAST, 2024) plans for learner variability from the start. It offers multiple means of engagement, representation, and action and expression, instead of adapting for individuals afterwards.
VideoTitle: CAST: UDL at a Glance (uploaded by College STAR)
WatchOutFor:
Offering choice without clear success criteria.
Assuming a written answer is required when the specification does not say so.
PracticeScenario: The assessment criterion is "explain the safe isolation procedure". Does the explanation have to be written?
PracticeAnswer: Not unless writing is what is being assessed. Check the awarding body specification. A recorded explanation or a demonstration may be acceptable evidence.
Keywords: autonomy captions dictation dyslexia eal esol flipped hearing immersive independence independent reader reading scaffold self writing

Title: Flipped theory: learners prepare, you facilitate
Summary: Learners meet the theory before the lesson. Lesson time goes on applying it, with you as facilitator and expert.
WhyItWorks: Flipped learning (Bergmann and Sams, 2012) moves explanation out of the lesson so more time goes on guided and independent practice, Rosenshine's later principles. It depends on accessible recordings and a quick check, so it builds on Foundations and Inclusion practice.
Frameworks: Rosenshine 5 and 9; UDL; Digital Skills Framework
WatchOutFor:
Videos that are too long. Keep each one to one idea.
No plan for learners who could not watch beforehand.
PracticeScenario: A third of the group arrive without having watched the video. What do you do?
PracticeAnswer: Start them on the video in class, with headphones and captions, while the others begin applying it. Check how learners access it at home and adjust.
Keywords: autonomy flipped independence independent scaffold self

Title: Learners ask the questions
Summary: Use the Question Formulation Technique so learners generate, improve and prioritise their own questions, which then drive the learning.
WhyItWorks: The Question Formulation Technique (Rothstein and Santana, 2011) teaches learners to produce, improve and prioritise their own questions. It shifts questioning from the teacher to the learner, building curiosity and independence.
WatchOutFor:
Turning the focus into a question yourself.
Judging questions while learners are still producing them.
PracticeScenario: Learners only write closed questions such as "Is it safe?". How do you move them on?
PracticeAnswer: That is expected at first. In the improve stage, ask them to change a closed question into an open one, for example "What makes it safe?", and discuss what each type is good for.
Keywords: answer class collaboration confident enquiry hands innovation learner-led project questioning questions quiet real up whole world

Title: Use Copilot to make a resource more accessible, then check it
Summary: Use Microsoft Copilot to simplify text or draft alt text, then check every output before it reaches a learner.
WhyItWorks: AI can produce a plain-language version or a first draft of alt text faster than writing by hand. It can also produce confident text that is wrong. Your professional judgement is what makes it safe to use.
Frameworks: Digital Skills Framework: AI literacy; WCAG 2.2 AA
WatchOutFor:
Publishing AI output without reading it in full.
Accepting AI-written alt text that describes the picture but misses the teaching point.
PracticeScenario: Copilot's plain-English version of your safety handout leaves out one of the five isolation steps. What went wrong, and what is your rule?
PracticeAnswer: AI can drop or change content. Always check the output line by line against the original, and never publish safety content you have not checked.

Title: A real-world project with 21st Century Learning Design
Summary: Learners solve a real problem for a real audience. The accessible, inclusive groundwork is built in, so the innovation is achievable.
WhyItWorks: 21st Century Learning Design (21CLD) came from Microsoft's Innovative Teaching and Learning research. Its rubrics describe six dimensions: collaboration, knowledge construction, self-regulation, real-world problem solving and innovation, use of ICT for learning, and skilled communication.
WatchOutFor:
A "real-world" project with no real audience.
Group work where one learner does everything.
PracticeScenario: Your project group has one learner doing all the work. Which 21CLD idea helps, and how?
PracticeAnswer: Collaboration, specifically shared responsibility and interdependence. Design tasks so each role is needed for the final product, and track milestones per role.
Keywords: collaboration enquiry innovation learner-led project questions real world
